newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine navy man tells of Dirty War baby theft.
newsitem.headline: Argentine navy man tells of Dirty War baby theft.

text.p: A former Argentine Navy officer who shocked the country in 1995 with tales of "death flights" in the Dirty War told a court on Friday that babies born to Navy prisoners were systematically stolen for adoption.

Adolfo Scilingo's televised confession of his work in the Naval Mechanical School, the biggest torture centre of the 1976-83 military dictatorship, triggered a historic wave of "mea culpas" from the modern forces in 1995.

The ex-captain, stripped of his rank like all convicted Dirty War officers, was back in the limelight on Friday when he gave evidence to a court investigating the abduction of 300 children born in clandestine military detention centres.
"For supposedly humanitarian reasons, it was decided all mothers to be detained there should give birth before being transferred," read his declaration, given to the media.
"Transferred" was the military euphemism for execution.
"To avoid their children being 'contaminated with extremist ideas' they should be adopted by 'normal' families -- that is, by Navy personnel," it continued.

Scilingo accused President Carlos Menem and Navy top brass of failing to act on evidence he sent them in 1995 about the abduction of children -- crimes not covered by amnesties for Dirty War crimes decreed under democracy in the 1980s.

"I don't understand the silence adopted by President Menem and the last Navy chiefs of staff, who should have gone to the courts when they found out about these crimes," he told reporters at the Buenos Aires Federal Court.

Scilingo accused Navy officers ,including former Adm. Emilio Massera, one of the leaders of the 1976 military coup, of running a racket in babies born in Navy jails. He urged the court to question 81 officers he said were in on the racket.
"It was all carried out with the blessing of the man who ran the (Navy School) directly, the commander-in-chief of the Navy, Emilio Massera," Scilingo's declaration said.

Scilingo has corroborated human rights investigations that show 4,400 people "disappeared" after being taken to the Navy Mechanics School. Many of them, too weak from torture to walk, were drugged, put in planes and thrown into the ocean.

The death toll of the campaign against leftist guerrillas and anyone suspected of sympathising is still unclear. About 3,000 deaths were confirmed but there are 10,000 official "desaparecidos" -- people abducted by the military and never seen again. Human rights groups say 30,000 disappeared.

Dirty War military men were tried and jailed after the restoration of democracy in 1983, but are now free because of the amnesties. But the amnesty did not cover crimes against children, and Federal Judge Adolfo Bagnasco is now investigating whether anyone can be charged with an organised campaign to "expropriate" children.
